title: Pinocchio is in danger of being fried in a pan like a fish.
paragraphs: During that desperate race there was one terrible moment, a moment when Pinocchio thought he was lost: because you must know that Alidoro (that was the mastiff’s name), by running and running, had almost caught him.
It is enough to say that the puppet could hear the fierce animal panting behind him, only a hand’s width away, and could even feel the hot blasts of his breath.
Luckily the beach was now close, and the sea was only a few steps away.

As soon as he reached the beach, the puppet made a splendid leap, just as a frog might, and landed in the water. Alidoro, instead, wanted to stop: but the force of his run carried him into the water too. And the poor creature could not swim; so he immediately began flailing his paws to stay afloat; but the more he flailed, the more his head went underwater.
When he managed to get his head out again, the poor dog’s eyes were wild with fear, and he barked and cried:
“I’m drowning! I’m drowning!”
“Then die!” Pinocchio answered from far away, now feeling safe from all danger.
“Help me, dear Pinocchio!… Save me from death!…”
At those heartbreaking cries, the puppet, who deep down had a very good heart, felt sorry for him, and turning to the dog, said:
“But if I help save you, do you promise not to bother me or chase me any more?”
“I promise! I promise! Hurry, please, because if you wait another half-minute, I’ll be dead.”

Pinocchio hesitated a little: but then, remembering that his father had told him many times that you never lose by doing a good deed, he swam over to Alidoro, and taking hold of his tail with both hands, brought him safe and sound onto the dry sand of the shore.

The poor dog could no longer stand. Without meaning to, he had swallowed so much salt water that he was swollen like a balloon. But the puppet, not wanting to trust him too much, thought it wise to jump back into the sea; and swimming away from the beach, he called to the friend he had saved:
“Goodbye, Alidoro; have a good journey, and give my greetings to everyone at home.”

“Goodbye, Pinocchio,” answered the dog, “a thousand thanks for saving me from death. You’ve done me a great favour: and in this world, what is done is repaid. If the chance comes, we’ll speak of it again…”

Pinocchio kept swimming, always staying near the land. At last he thought he had reached a safe place: and glancing at the shore, he saw a sort of cave among the rocks, with a long plume of smoke coming out of it.
“There must be a fire in that cave,” he said to himself. “All the better! I’ll go and dry myself and get warm, and then?… And then whatever happens will happen.”

Having made up his mind, he went towards the rocks; but just as he was about to climb up, he felt something underwater rising, rising, rising, and lifting him into the air. He immediately tried to escape, but it was too late now, because to his great surprise he found himself trapped inside a big net among a mass of fish of every shape and size, wagging their tails and struggling like so many desperate souls.

At the same time he saw a fisherman come out of the cave, so ugly, so very ugly, that he looked like a sea monster. Instead of hair, he had a thick bush of green grass on his head; the skin of his body was green, his eyes were green, and his very long beard, reaching all the way down here, was green too. He looked like a large green lizard standing on its hind legs.
When the fisherman had pulled the net out of the sea, he cried happily:
“Blessed Providence! Today too I’ll be able to feast on fish!”
“Good thing I’m not a fish!” Pinocchio said to himself, feeling a little braver.
The net full of fish was carried into the cave, a dark, smoky cave with a great frying pan of oil sizzling in the middle, giving off a smell like burnt candle wicks that took your breath away.
“Now let’s see what fish we’ve caught!” said the green fisherman; and pushing a huge hand into the net, a hand as large as a baker’s shovel, he pulled out a handful of red mullet.
“Lovely red mullet!” he said, looking at them and sniffing them happily. And after sniffing them, he threw them into a tub with no water in it.
Then he repeated the same thing several times; and as he pulled out the other fish, his mouth watered, and he said with delight:
“Lovely hake!…”
“Wonderful grey mullet!…”
“Delicious sole!…”
“Splendid young sea bass!…”
“Pretty little anchovies, heads and all!”
As you can imagine, the hake, grey mullet, sole, young sea bass, and anchovies all went in a heap into the tub to keep the red mullet company.
The last one left in the net was Pinocchio.
As soon as the fisherman pulled him out, he opened his great green eyes wide with surprise and cried, almost frightened:
“What kind of fish is this? I don’t remember ever eating a fish shaped like this.”
And he looked at him carefully again, and after examining him closely from every side, he finally said:
“I see; it must be a sea crab.”
Then Pinocchio, upset at being mistaken for a crab, said crossly:
“What do you mean, a crab? Look how you’re treating me! For your information, I’m a puppet.”
“A puppet?” repeated the fisherman. “To tell the truth, a puppet-fish is a new fish to me! All the better! I’ll enjoy eating you even more.”
“Eat me? But can’t you understand that I’m not a fish? Can’t you hear that I talk and think just as you do?”
“That’s quite true,” added the fisherman, “and since I see you’re a fish, and you’re lucky enough to talk and think like me, I want to show you proper respect too.”
“And what sort of respect would that be?…”
“As a sign of friendship and special respect, I’ll let you choose how you want to be cooked. Would you like to be fried in the pan, or would you rather be cooked in a pot with tomato sauce?”
“To tell the truth,” answered Pinocchio, “if I’m to choose, I’d much rather be set free so I can go home.”

“You’re joking! Do you think I want to lose the chance to taste such a rare fish? A puppet-fish doesn’t turn up in these seas every day. Leave it to me: I’ll fry you in the pan with all the other fish, and you’ll be pleased. Being fried in company is always a comfort.”

At this speech, poor Pinocchio began crying, screaming, and begging: and as he cried he said: “How much better it would have been if I’d gone to school!… I chose to listen to my friends, and now I’m paying for it!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!…”

And because he wriggled like an eel and struggled with all his might to slip from the green fisherman’s claws, the fisherman took a good strip of rush fibre and, after tying his hands and feet like a sausage, threw him into the bottom of the tub with the others.
Then, taking out a rough wooden tray full of flour, he began coating all the fish in flour: and as he coated each one, he threw it into the pan to fry.

The first to dance in the boiling oil were the poor hake: then came the young sea bass, then the grey mullet, then the sole and anchovies, and then it was Pinocchio’s turn. Seeing himself so close to death (and such a horrible death!), he shook so much and was so frightened that he had neither voice nor breath left to beg.

The poor boy begged with his eyes! But the green fisherman, without even noticing, rolled him five or six times in the flour, covering him so thoroughly from head to foot that he looked like a puppet made of plaster.
Then he took him by the head, and…
